Talks between Brazil’s Braskem SA and its creditors regarding an out-of-court debt rework have soured, with shareholders taking a proposed capital injection key to a deal off the table if talks stand as they are, according to people familiar with the matter.
After meetings with creditors in New York this week, shareholders decided to go back on a pledge to inject capital into Braskem after bondholders rejected a proposal that included $3.8 billion in debt conversion, the people said, asking not to be named discussing private matters. Negotiations are still ongoing and no final decision has been made.

item.title: AI-Generated Movie Heading Theaters
item.description:
BusinessWeek Radio Simulcast • Nov 6th, 2026
AI-Generated Movie Heading Theaters
Artificial intelligence is moving from experimental videos to the big screen. Fable Studio CEO Edward Saatchi says a team of just 30 people spent nine months creating Gods Don’t Give Gifts, an AI-generated animated feature that still relies on human directors, writers, voice actors and artists. He joins Bloomberg Businessweek Daily to discuss how AI changes the filmmaking process and what it means for Hollywood's traditional production model.

Takeaways by Bloomberg AI
The Canadian dollar posted its biggest weekly loss since late September after weaker-than-expected domestic employment data reinforced concerns about the outlook for the country’s economy.
The loonie fell 0.8% on Friday against a broadly stronger US dollar, bringing its weekly decline to 1.1%. The currency extended losses after data showed Canada’s unemployment rate edged up to 6.7% in October, while employment fell by 4,700 for a third straight month of job losses.

Hedge funds cut bullish crude bets by the most since June as the US and Iran struck rare de-escalatory notes, positioning them to profit from the selloff after the Democratic sweep of Congress.
Money managers decreased their combined net-long positions on the West Texas Intermediate and Brent benchmarks by 78,492 lots to 272,075 lots in the week through Nov. 3, according to data from ICE Futures Europe and the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission compiled by Bloomberg. That’s the biggest drop since this summer, around when the US and Iran agreed to an interim deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Gold fell after a hot US nonfarm payrolls print added fuel to speculations that the Federal Reserve will seek to raise interest rates to contain inflation.
Bullion slipped as much as 1.5% toward $4,020 an ounce after the report. Traders also weighed diplomatic efforts to end the Middle East conflict against sharp losses in the artificial intelligence trade that have bruised risk appetite.

Takeaways by Bloomberg AI
Months of unease over Wall Street’s artificial-intelligence boom erupted into a global market convulsion this week, opening a dangerous new chapter for the investment frenzy that has helped power stock prices, corporate spending and economic growth.
The worries have been on display all year: stretched valuations, mounting debt and doubts about the payoff from trillions of dollars in AI spending. But the Democratic sweep of Congress has added a new political threat, raising the prospect of restrictions on the vast data-center buildout underpinning the boom.

A rebound in chipmakers propped up the stock market as dip buyers emerged despite economic data that reinforced speculation the Federal Reserve will boost rates in December.
In the wake of a rout that jolted Wall Street, the Nasdaq 100 climbed 1.35%. A gauge of chip giants jumped 4.2%. Tech shares also lifted the S&P 500 even as most of its firms fell. Treasury yields and the dollar rose.
